strengths: The paper targets a real and important bottleneck: 3D Gaussian Splatting training is computationally expensive, and a faster, more memory-efficient training framework is practically valuable.

The profiling-driven motivation is concrete: it identifies backward rasterization, atomicAdd contention, declining L2 cache hit rate, and redundant tile/patch computation, which supports the proposed optimizations.
The reported speedups are substantial: 3.4x over the original 3DGS and 1.4x over a TamingGS-integrated baseline on Mip-NeRF 360, evaluated on both A100 and RTX3090 GPUs.

Several components are technically reasonable and well motivated, including Morton-code-based clustering/compacting, cluster-level culling, sparse gradients, tighter 2D AABBs, 8x8 tiles, and multibatch reduction via shared memory.
The paper attempts to maintain quality alongside speed, reporting PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS results that are mostly comparable or slightly better than the baseline.
The proposed modular design with Python and CUDA APIs, even if incomplete for rasterization, could improve prototyping and extensibility relative to the original monolithic 3DGS codebase.
The manuscript provides algorithm pseudocode for multibatch reduction and compact gradient handling, which helps clarify the intended implementation.
weaknesses: The contribution is primarily engineering integration rather than a new algorithm: it combines known ideas such as Morton sorting, tile-based rendering, sparse gradients, AABB culling, and parallel reduction into 3DGS, with limited algorithmic novelty for a top-tier vision venue.

The most relevant prior work, gsplat, is a modular 3DGS library with training optimizations, but it is not compared experimentally despite being directly related; this substantially weakens the claimed novelty and practical advantage.
The abstract claims approximately 30% GPU memory reduction, but no memory benchmark, measurement methodology, or table/figure substantiates this claim in the evaluation.

The evaluation lacks ablation studies that isolate the end-to-end contribution of each component (clustering, compacting, sparse gradients, 8x8 tiles, reduction). It is therefore unclear which optimizations drive the speedup and by how much.

Quality comparisons are potentially confounded: the authors mention SfM/COLMAP processing and parameter adjustments, but it is not fully clear that LiteGS and all baselines use identical data preprocessing and training settings. Single-run results without error bars further weaken the evidence.
The modularity and dual-API claims are overstated: rasterization is CUDA-only, so the core bottleneck cannot be customized through the Python API, limiting the flexibility contribution.

Method details are insufficient for reproducibility: cluster construction/culling/compacting specifics, sparse-gradient correctness, re-blocking frequency, tile-size trade-offs, and hyperparameters are not fully described. The source code URL appears blank in the manuscript.

The presentation is rough: grammar and typographical errors, vague or missing figure captions (e.g., Figure 1), undefined profiling terms (MIO, LG throttle), and an incomplete reference for Morton's method reduce clarity.
The paper does not discuss limitations or societal impact, and it does not adequately address the trade-offs of its design choices, such as the larger visibility table caused by 8x8 tiles.
Baseline naming and protocol are unclear: '3DGS-T' and the TamingGS-integrated baseline are not precisely defined, making the reported 1.4x speedup harder to interpret.

Assessed as an Applied/Systems contribution rather than Algorithms/General, the work has practical value but still needs stronger evidence, broader comparison, and clearer reproducibility to meet ECCV standards.

strengths: The paper targets a practically important and timely problem: the training efficiency and usability of 3D Gaussian Splatting, which is currently one of the most widely used scene-reconstruction representations. A faster, more memory-efficient, and more modifiable training framework would benefit a large portion of the vision community.

The motivation analysis is well grounded in profiling evidence. The authors present function-level execution-time breakdowns (Fig. 2), warp-state sampling (Fig. 3, Table 1), L2 cache hit rates (Fig. 4), and patch/fragment statistics (Figs. 6, 7), which concretely identify the backward rasterization, memory-access locality, and redundant-computation bottlenecks. This diagnostic portion is arguably the most valuable part of the submission.

The reported results are substantial and consistent across two GPUs (A100 and RTX3090): roughly 3.4x end-to-end training speedup over the original 3DGS and ~1.4x over the Taming-GS-integrated variant (Table 2), together with a claimed ~30% GPU memory reduction. Speedups hold across all nine Mip-NeRF 360 scenes.

The modular decomposition (cluster culling, cluster compaction, projection, binning, rasterization) with a Python/autograd API for prototyping and a Torch CUDA extension API for production is a reasonable and useful design, and the paper does a good job explaining why a Python rasterization path is impractical.

Quality preservation is checked rather than assumed: Table 3 reports SSIM, PSNR, and LPIPS against the 3DGS baseline, and the authors report that SfM/COLMAP preprocessing was adjusted to obtain fair baselines, which is a level of care often missing in efficiency papers.

The discussion of the sparse-gradient attribution in Taming-GS (Sec. 4.4) is an insightful, honest technical observation (the acceleration comes largely from the fused Adam optimizer, not sparsity), which is a genuinely useful correction for the community.

The individual optimizations (Morton-code reordering, 128-point blocks, cluster-level frustum culling, tighter AABBs considering both axes and transparency, 8x8 tiles, shared-memory multi-batch reduction, and compaction of valid gradients) are sensible and mutually reinforcing, and the reasoning behind each design choice is clearly explained.
weaknesses: The manuscript appears incomplete in ways that affect verifiability. Figure 1's caption is literally '...' with no description of the axes or the quantitative basis for the placement of LiteGS, and the source-code URL in Sec. 4 is left blank ('The full source code is available at ____'). For a framework/systems contribution whose central claims are speed and usability, the absence of an accessible implementation and a meaningful summary figure substantially weakens the case.

There is no ablation study isolating the contribution of each component. Given the number of stacked optimizations (cluster culling, compaction, sparse gradients, tighter AABB, 8x8 tiling, multi-batch reduction, gradient compaction, fused Adam), it is impossible to tell from the presented evidence which techniques account for the 3.4x/1.4x gains. This is especially important because some components (e.g., sparse gradients) are explicitly described as borrowed from Taming-GS.

The baseline set is narrow. The paper compares only against original 3DGS and a Taming-GS-integrated 3DGS, despite discussing several efficiency- or library-oriented works in related work (Distwar [5], gsplat [22], OctreeGS, LightGaussian [6], compressed grids [14]). In particular, gsplat [22] is acknowledged as an existing modular, usability-focused 3DGS library, yet no head-to-head comparison (speed, memory, or API expressiveness) is provided, so the claimed modularity/usability advantage over prior libraries is unsubstantiated.

The novelty is incremental relative to the systems literature. Most individual techniques (Morton sorting for locality, cluster-level culling, tighter AABBs, shared-memory reduction, fused optimizers) are standard GPU-optimization patterns applied to 3DGS. The contribution is primarily an engineering integration rather than a new algorithmic or theoretical insight, which should be reflected in how strongly the claims are framed.

The paper's central 'modularity' claim is under-evidenced. Aside from the dual Python/CUDA API and the splitting of stages into extension functions, there is little demonstration that the modular design actually enables the claimed 'straightforward customization of new ideas' (e.g., a case study implementing a novel variant using the API). The abstract's assertion of flexibility is therefore not directly supported.

Evaluation is limited to a single dataset (Mip-NeRF 360) and only reports training-time and quality metrics; there is no measurement of memory usage in a table (the ~30% figure is only in the abstract/introduction), no runtime/inference comparison, no measurement of the Python-API overhead, and no statistics on variance across runs. The Table 2 layout (A100/3090 as row headers with 3DGS/3DGS-T/LiteGS as sub-rows) is also confusingly formatted.

Some technical claims are asserted rather than demonstrated. For example, the paper claims that using 8x8 tiles 'significantly reduces the total number of fragments' and that LiteGS's binning optimizations make the larger visibility table worthwhile, but the net effect on binning cost is not quantified; likewise, the claim that the cluster-and-compact method 'minimizes warp divergence' is not directly measured.

strengths: Tackles a practically relevant problem—training-time efficiency and usability of 3DGS—and grounds it in real profiling: Figures 2–4 and Table 1 quantify that the backward rasterization pass dominates training, that warp cycles per issued instruction start at ~132 and only fall to ~34, and that L2 hit rate degrades from 93.8% to 36.9% over training. This bottleneck analysis is concrete and useful.

The system is actually built and delivers measurable wall-clock gains: Table 2 reports roughly 2.8–3.9x speedup over 3DGS on A100 (e.g., bicycle 31:22 to 08:04) and ~1.1–1.8x over the TamingGS-integrated 3DGS, with quality metrics in Table 3 (SSIM/PSNR/LPIPS) comparable or marginally better, so the speedups do not obviously come at a quality cost.

The individual engineering choices are sensible and mutually reinforcing: Morton-code re-blocking of 128-point chunks, cluster-level frustum culling followed by compaction into contiguous memory, shared-memory multi-batch gradient reduction to avoid global AtomicAdd contention, and 8x8 tiles for the many tiny Gaussians that appear late in training. Figures 5–7 provide supporting micro-evidence (L2 hit rate preserved with cluster+compact, ~40% fewer patches, markedly fewer fragments at 8x8).

Section 4.4 offers a useful, non-obvious observation: the speedup attributed to sparse gradients in Taming-GS is likely dominated by fused Adam rather than sparsity itself, and the authors correctly reason about tensor shapes to justify this. This kind of candid technical critique is valuable to the community.

The dual-API design (Python/autograd for prototyping, CUDA extension for production) is a plausible usability contribution, and the paper is explicit that the rasterization module only ships in CUDA because the Python version was too slow—an honest limitation statement.
weaknesses: The single most relevant baseline is never evaluated. gsplat [22] is cited as the only prior modular 3DGS library with training-speed optimizations, and it overlaps substantially with LiteGS (chunked/Morton sorting, culling, sparse gradients, fused Adam, dual Python/CUDA API). Not benchmarking against it—nor against Distwar [5]—leaves the central 'high-performance modular framework' claim unsupported.

There is no ablation. The paper proposes at least five optimizations (cluster culling, compacting, 8x8 tiles, multi-batch reduction, sparse gradient/fused Adam, tighter AABB) plus a changed density-control schedule ('reducing the frequency of point management operations while performing larger-scale additions or deletions'), yet no table decomposes the end-to-end speedup by component. Figures 5–7 report only proxy statistics (L2 hit rate, patch counts, fragment counts), not wall-clock contributions, so the reader cannot tell which ideas actually matter.

The abstract's '~30% GPU memory reduction' is never substantiated. Section 5 reports only training time and PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS; there is no memory table, no per-scene measurement, and no methodology. A headline claim in the abstract has zero supporting evidence in the paper.

The baseline setup is confounded and non-comparable. The authors state they modified SfM/COLMAP processing and adjusted parameters so that their 3DGS numbers exceed published values, which breaks comparability with the literature and with their own reference points. Conversely, the '3DGS' column omits the fused-Adam/sparse-gradient machinery that the authors themselves argue (Sec. 4.4) drives most of TamingGS's gains, so the headline 3.4x partly reflects an optimizer-level difference rather than a rasterization improvement; the more meaningful 1.4x-vs-TamingGS number is downplayed in the abstract.

Novelty is largely integration of known techniques, and the paper does not delineate what is new. Sparse gradients are explicitly adopted from Taming-GS [13], and Morton sorting, frustum culling, tile AABBs, and fused optimizers are standard practice. The pipeline steps in Sec. 4.1 carry no citations, so attribution of each borrowed idea is unclear, and the 'modular design' claim is asserted rather than demonstrated (no user study, no worked extension example, no measurement of Python-API overhead or of the claimed prototyping benefit).

Evaluation breadth is thin for a systems contribution: a single dataset (Mip-NeRF 360), a single task (static novel-view-synthesis training), no memory or inference measurements, no per-iteration timing or convergence curves, no reported number of Gaussians, no repeated runs or variance, no additional benchmarks (e.g., Tanks & Temples, Deep Blending, outdoor/large-scale scenes), and no failure cases.

Several claims overreach the evidence. 'LiteGS retains the core 3DGS algorithm' contradicts the modified density control, tile size, and bounding boxes. Figure 1—a hand-drawn schematic with 'Features/Speed/Modular' axes—is used to assert that LiteGS 'substantially outperforms prior approaches in terms of training speed,' which such a figure cannot support. The 2D-AABB discussion raises a two-pass/one-pass accuracy-speed trade-off but never states which variant the final system uses.

Clarity, rigor, and reproducibility problems: the Figure 1 caption is a literal placeholder ('Figure 1: ...'); the code release is a blank placeholder ('The full source code is available at .'); there are grammar/typo issues ('do not solving all performance bottlenecks', 'we use more tricks', 'The simgling result', 'Modular Designed'); naming is inconsistent ('LiteGS' vs 'LiteGS'); and the experimental protocol (hardware/software versions, iteration counts, seeds, timing methodology, which 3DGS/TamingGS revision and which flags were enabled) is unspecified, so the reported timings cannot be reproduced or audited.

strengths: The paper provides a comprehensive, well-motivated analysis of 3DGS training bottlenecks at three distinct levels (GPU computation, data management, and densification), and proposes targeted solutions for each, which is a coherent system-and-algorithm co-design rather than a collection of unrelated tricks.

Strong and clearly validated empirical results: Table 1 shows substantial speedups (up to 13.4x vs. original 3DGS and up to 1.4x vs. Mini-Splatting v2 for lightweight models) while maintaining comparable or superior reconstruction quality, with consistent gains across three standard benchmarks (Mip-NeRF360, Tanks&Temples, Deep Blending).

Novel algorithmic contributions are well-motivated: the opacity gradient variance densification metric explicitly addresses a real ambiguity in the original gradient-magnitude criterion, and the opacity decay mechanism is a principled replacement for hard resets; both are validated in Table 4.

The scanline reformulation of the 2D Gaussian evaluation as a quadratic polynomial in pixel offset is elegant, reduces register pressure and the number of multiplications from 9 to 3, and is a genuinely useful technical insight for efficient splatting.

Thorough ablation studies isolate the contributions of the Cluster-Cull-Compact pipeline (Table 2, ~36% training time reduction with negligible quality loss) and of each densification component (Table 4).

The warp-based rasterizer design ('one warp per tile') with single warp-level reduction per tile is a clean and effective solution to the atomic-add overhead, and Table 3 provides clear operator-level breakdown evidence (7-13x over atomic rasterizer).
The framework is open-sourced, which supports reproducibility and community adoption.
The paper is well-organized, with clear motivation, technical exposition, and readable presentation of results.
weaknesses: Comparison fairness across methods is somewhat muddled: baselines use different iteration counts (some at 40K per the Table 1 footnote, LiteGS at 30K, LiteGS-turbo at 18K), which makes it difficult to attribute performance differences purely to the proposed techniques. A more controlled comparison at matched iterations for all methods would strengthen the claims.

The title's 'Subminutes' claim is somewhat overstated for the general case: the fastest full training reported is ~111-145s (~2 minutes) on an RTX 3090, and sub-minute performance is only suggested for hypothetical future GPUs (e.g., RTX 5090). The claim should be softened or more carefully qualified.

Experiments are conducted only on a single GPU (RTX 3090), yet the paper makes broad claims about hardware-aware efficiency; the generalizability of the warp-reduce, register-pressure, and tile-size findings to other GPU architectures (e.g., AMD, Hopper/Blackwell) is not demonstrated.
The claimed memory-footprint advantage ('lower peak memory footprint') is asserted as a benefit of LiteGS over Mini-Splatting but is not quantified with actual peak-memory measurements.
No explicit limitations or societal-impact discussion is provided, despite the paper introducing a new acceleration framework with potential broader implications.

The computational cost of the proposed variance-based densification metric (sum of squared gradients, sum of gradients, fragment count per primitive) is not analyzed in detail, even though it is claimed to be cheap; a complexity/overhead comparison would be useful.

The four-step integer warp-reduce trick for floating-point accumulation (find max exponent, align mantissas, integer warp-reduce-add, reconstruct) is an unusual workaround whose numerical accuracy and error behavior are not discussed.

The 'new accuracy record' claim (e.g., 'LiteGS sets a new accuracy record') is based on relatively modest SSIM/PSNR improvements over 3DGS-MCMC and SSS, and it is unclear whether these are statistically significant or within noise; error bars or multiple-run statistics are absent.

While individual components (Morton coding, cluster culling, warp-level reduction, FP16 blending) are adaptations of existing techniques, the paper could more clearly delineate which aspects are genuinely novel versus engineering integration.

strengths: Addresses a critical bottleneck in 3D Gaussian Splatting training with a comprehensive system-algorithm co-design approach spanning low-level GPU optimization, mid-level data management, and high-level algorithm design.

Proposes a novel warp-based rasterizer with 'one warp per tile', a scanline algorithm, and strategic mixed-precision computing, significantly reducing gradient reduction overhead and improving GPU utilization.
Introduces a Cluster-Cull-Compact pipeline using Morton coding for dynamic spatial sorting, effectively improving data locality, reducing cache misses and warp divergence.
Develops a robust densification metric based on opacity gradient variance, resolving ambiguity in the original 3DGS heuristic, and a stable opacity decay mechanism to enhance reconstruction quality.

Extensive experiments on three standard datasets (Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks & Temples, Deep Blending) against multiple baselines demonstrate up to 13.4x speedup for lightweight models and ~6x for high-quality reconstruction, with comparable or superior quality.
Ablation studies isolate and validate the contribution of each proposed component, including the Cluster-Cull-Compact pipeline, warp-based rasterizer, and densification strategy.
Code is open-sourced, facilitating reproducibility and adoption by the community.
The paper is well-structured, clearly written, and provides sufficient implementation details for reproduction.
weaknesses: The individual techniques (warp-based rasterization, Morton coding, scanline algorithm, mixed precision) are largely adaptations of existing methods; the primary novelty lies in their integration and tuning rather than fundamental algorithmic innovation.

Some claims are slightly overstated: the 'order of magnitude' speedup for high-quality reconstruction is approximately 6x in practice, and the abstract could be more precise about the range of speedups.
Table 1 likely contains a typo: the 'Num' value for 3DGS-MCMC (3.21) appears inconsistent with other entries and the text, possibly missing a factor of 1000, which could confuse readers.

Hyperparameter choices (e.g., opacity decay rate, densification interval, tile size) may require per-scene tuning; the paper does not provide sensitivity analysis to demonstrate robustness across diverse scenes.
Evaluation is limited to three standard datasets; testing on more varied scenes (e.g., synthetic, indoor, outdoor with different lighting) would strengthen generalization claims.
No theoretical analysis or complexity guarantees are provided for the proposed densification metric, which is heuristic in nature.
Societal impact and potential negative consequences are not discussed, though this is not a critical requirement for a systems-oriented paper.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important and practical bottleneck (3DGS training cost) with a coherent, multi-level co-design spanning the CUDA kernel (warp-per-tile rasterization, intra-thread + single warp-level reduction), the data layout (Morton-code cluster-cull-compact, cluster-granularity sparse updates), and the densification rule. The problem framing (gradient-reduction conflicts, poor spatial locality, non-robust densification) is well motivated in Section 1.

Reports substantial and consistent wall-clock gains across three standard benchmarks (Mip-NeRF360, Tanks&Temples, Deep Blending): up to ~13x over the original 3DGS, ~3x on average over TamingGS, and ~1.4x over Mini-Splatting v2, with several operating points (turbo/balance/quality) that give a useful speed-quality Pareto front. The framework is claimed to be open-sourced, which supports reproducibility.

The ablation studies are reasonably designed and largely support the individual components: Table 2 isolates the Cluster-Cull-Compact pipeline (36% training-time reduction with negligible quality change), Table 3 isolates the rasterizer at multiple primitive counts (7-13x vs. the atomic baseline, ~4x vs. per-splat, 1.5x vs. TC-GS), and Table 4 isolates the opacity decay and the gradient-variance criterion (each worth roughly 0.3-0.4 dB PSNR).

Attribution is mostly handled properly: Morton/Z-order coding, cluster-cull-compact, scanline evaluation of the quadratic Gaussian, mixed-precision blending, and prior densification heuristics (ADC, EDC, TamingGS score-based, PUP-3DGS) are cited to their sources rather than presented as new, and the proposed opacity-decay substitute for hard opacity reset is a cheap, plausible, and empirically validated modification.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty relative to the claims. The components are largely adaptations or combinations of known ideas: warp/block-level reduction for gradient accumulation (cf. DISTWAR and TamingGS's per-splat parallelism), Morton-code cluster-cull-compact explicitly adapted from real-time rendering (Laine et al., Hapala et al.), scanline evaluation of the quadratic Gaussian from classic graphics texts (Foley; Shirley), FP16 mixed precision already explored in TamingGS, and variance/error-based densification related to EDC, PUP-3DGS and score-based selection. The paper does not isolate what is fundamentally new beyond careful engineering integration, so it reads as a systems-engineering exercise with incremental algorithmic content.

The headline accuracy claim is not supported. The abstract and conclusion state that LiteGS 'sets a new accuracy record' / 'sets a new SOTA for quality', but the baseline set is narrow (3DGS, 3DGS-MCMC, SSS, TamingGS, Mini-Splatting v1/v2) and excludes many strong recent 3DGS variants as well as already-optimized 3DGS implementations/libraries (e.g., gsplat) that likely contain several of the same kernel-level optimizations. Against the strongest quality baseline (3DGS-MCMC) the gain is marginal (28.25 vs. 28.08 dB PSNR, with SSIM 0.836 vs. 0.834 and LPIPS 0.176 vs. 0.186), which is within run-to-run variation, so 'new accuracy record' is an overclaim.

The speed claims are confounded and, in places, inconsistent with the evidence. The 13.4x figure combines system optimizations with algorithmic savings (fewer primitives, 18K vs. 30K iterations, different densification), so it is not a like-for-like acceleration of 3DGS; only Table 3 isolates the rasterizer, where the gain over the strongest system baseline (TC-GS) is ~1.5x. The title's 'in Subminutes' is also not achieved: the fastest reported runs are 108-145 s (Table 1), and the intro's '10.7x over the SOTA acceleration solution' does not match the reported TamingGS ratios (1.0-3.8x).

Experimental reporting contains internal inconsistencies and unresolved fairness issues. The Table 1 footnote is self-contradictory ('For a fair comparison, LiteGS uses the same number of iterations as SSS' and '* means the training iteration is 40K' versus the 30K iterations stated in 'Parameter Scale') and reports numbers (0.780/24.72/0.133, 398 s) that match no row in any table. It is never stated whether the baseline timings (e.g., 3DGS-MCMC 3142 s, SSS 3961 s) were re-measured on the same RTX 3090 or copied from other papers run on different hardware; without this, the central timing comparison is unverifiable.

All evidence comes from a single GPU (RTX 3090), while the core contributions are explicitly hardware-specific: Ampere warp-reduce integer instructions, register-pressure/occupancy tuning, and a 4x32=128-pixel tile chosen for a particular register file. There is no portability study, no occupancy/roofline analysis, no evidence for the claim that 128 pixels 'fits the major NVIDIA GPUs', and the asserted lower peak-memory advantage for memory-limited devices is never measured. The one-warp-per-tile design also raises unaddressed occupancy concerns for small images or for GPUs with fewer/more SMs.

The proposed densification criterion is under-analyzed. The quantity C_i x Var = S_i - M_i^2/C_i is a sum of squared deviations (not a variance) and scales with the number of observing pixels C_i, biasing the metric toward well-observed primitives; the paper offers only an informal argument that high variance implies under-reconstruction, with no theoretical grounding, no sensitivity study of the new threshold, decay schedule, decay epoch count, or re-sort interval, and no comparison against other principled indicators (EDC, PUP-3DGS, score-based) under matched hyperparameters. Likewise, the integer-mantissa warp-reduce trick is presented without any numerical-error or precision-loss analysis.

Evidence is thin in places: Figure 1 shows only a single scene (garden), there are no qualitative/visual comparisons, no per-scene breakdowns, no failure cases, no large-scale or dynamic-scene evaluation, and no discussion of the method's limitations beyond a short future-work paragraph. Given the 14-page ECCV limit and the brevity of the related work, there is ample room to strengthen these points.
